blocks.heading: The thermostat
text: Between 2009 and today the hashing behind bitcoin grew by a factor in the trillions.
A block still takes about ten minutes. Nobody arranged that, and nobody can adjust it.

blocks.heading: Every 2016 blocks, everyone recomputes
text: 2016 blocks at ten minutes is exactly two weeks: **1,209,600 seconds**.
At the end of each window, every node looks at how long those blocks really took and scales the target by the ratio.

blocks.alt: Four bars diverging from a no-change line, showing difficulty multipliers for windows that took 10, 14, 20 and 70 days, the last one clamped
blocks.caption: Blocks arriving in ten days instead of fourteen make the next 2016 blocks **1.4x harder**.

blocks.question: Who computes this, and how does everyone end up with the same target when nobody announces it?
answer: Nobody computes it, in the sense of being in charge. Each node runs the same arithmetic on the same block headers it already stores.
There is no message, no vote, no announcement, and nothing to disagree about. Determinism is doing the coordination that a committee would otherwise have to do.

blocks.heading: With a hard limit on the swing
text: The measured timespan is clamped to between a quarter and four times the target before it is used.
So no single adjustment can change difficulty by more than a factor of four in either direction, whatever the timestamps claim.

blocks.heading: It counts 2015 gaps
text: The timespan is measured between the first and last blocks of the window. Between 2016 blocks there are 2015 intervals, not 2016.
So the target is set for a slightly faster network than intended:
About 0.05% fast, permanently. Fixing it means a hard fork to correct half a thousandth of the block interval, so it stays.
It has one visible consequence: halvings are counted in blocks, every 210,000 of them, so they arrive slightly earlier than "every four years" suggests.

blocks.heading: The thermostat is slow on purpose
text: It only reads the room every two weeks, and it can only turn the dial so far.
Which is fine when hashrate drifts upward, and much less fine when a large part of it disappears in a week.

blocks.heading: When a country switched off
text: Mining was banned in China, and a large share of the world's hashrate went offline in weeks.
Blocks slowed to well over ten minutes, so the window itself took longer to finish. The adjustment, when it arrived, cut difficulty by about **28%** - the largest drop in bitcoin's history.

blocks.title: The recovery is bounded too
text: Because a single adjustment cannot exceed a factor of four, a catastrophic loss of hashrate cannot be corrected in one step - and the slower the blocks, the longer the fix takes to arrive.
The system is stable, not responsive. Those are different properties.

There is no derivation. It is a trade: a block has to reach the whole network in a small fraction of the interval, or miners keep working on histories that are already stale and the work is thrown away.
Ten minutes was a conservative choice by one person in 2008. Everything since has been built on it.

blocks.heading: One sentence worth keeping
text: The block interval is not a property of the machines; it is a set point the network re-derives from its own history, twice a month, without speaking.
Nora still has not shipped the synthesiser. Next: exactly how sure she can be, expressed as a number.
